name: Tauri
vendor: The Tauri Programme within The Commons Conservancy
summary: A framework for desktop and mobile apps with a web front end shown in the operating system’s own web view and a Rust core that holds the app’s logic and its access to the system.
intro: A Tauri app has two halves. The front end is any web project that builds to HTML, CSS and JavaScript, including Rust compiled to WebAssembly with Leptos. Tauri doesn’t bundle a browser to show it. Its WRY library opens the web view the platform already has: WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS and iOS, WebKitGTK on Linux and the Android System WebView, while its TAO library creates the windows. The web view is linked at run time rather than shipped, which is why a minimal Tauri app can be smaller than 600 KB. Tauri serves the page through its own protocol, without starting a localhost web server.

The other half is the core process, a Rust binary and the only part with full access to the operating system. It owns windows, tray menus, notifications and global state such as database connections. The page calls Rust through commands: a function marked `#[tauri::command]` is registered with `generate_handler!` and called from JavaScript with `invoke()`, with arguments sent as JSON; `async` commands run off the UI thread. All messages pass through the core, and Tauri 2’s capabilities decide which windows may use which permissions, such as `core:window:allow-set-title`. Tauri 2.0 (October 2024) added iOS and Android, with native Swift and Kotlin plugins, and moved most features into official plugins. The current line is 2.12 (September 2026); Tauri 3 is in alpha. The bundler produces `.app` and `.dmg`, `.deb`, `.rpm` and AppImage, and `.msi` or NSIS `.exe` installers.
strengths: Small apps: no bundled browser, so installers are a few megabytes; Firezone’s clients are 8 MB on Windows and 12 MB on Linux, against about 100 MB for a default Electron app
Any web front end, plus a Rust back end for the work a browser can’t do, with commands that call async Rust and serialize arguments with `serde`
A guarded boundary: the web view reaches the system only through the core, and capabilities grant each window just the permissions it needs
Tray icons, notifications, deep links and self-updates come as built-in features or official plugins, and one project builds desktop and mobile apps
limits: Three rendering engines: the same HTML runs in WebView2, WKWebView and WebKitGTK, whose versions and features depend on the user’s system, so each platform needs testing
Linux packaging follows WebKitGTK: Tauri 2 needs webkit2gtk 4.1, and Firezone found no WebKitGTK version shared by Ubuntu 20.04, 22.04 and 24.04, so one `.deb` couldn’t cover all three
The web view still costs memory: Firezone’s GUI idles at about 100 MB of RAM with every window hidden
Back-end work beyond the provided plugins means writing Rust, and on mobile, Swift or Kotlin

story: Electron made desktop apps out of web apps by shipping Chromium and Node.js inside each one, which made even small apps large downloads. Tauri, begun in 2019, took the opposite approach: reuse the web view every operating system already has, and write the native side in Rust. Tauri 1.0 shipped on 19 June 2022, after nine months of betas and four of release candidates. The whole project had been audited by an independent firm, and the team placed the code under the Commons Conservancy so it couldn’t be taken away or locked behind paid features. The announcement argued for small apps in energy terms: 1,000 downloads of a 200 MB app move 200 GB, against 3 GB for a 3 MB one.

Tauri 2.0, after more than two years of work, became stable on 2 October 2024. It added iOS and Android, moved much of the core into plugins, replaced 1.x’s allowlist with permissions, scopes and capabilities, and rewrote the IPC layer to send raw payloads; Radically Open Security audited it during the beta. In March 2025 the team showed an experimental back end based on Verso, a browser built on Servo, with the long-term aim of a shared, evergreen engine apps wouldn’t have to bundle. In 2026 the 2.x line reached 2.12 and dropped Windows 7, and Tauri 3 entered alpha.

choices.choice: The system web view instead of a bundled browser
choices.why: Shipping a browser with every app costs download size, disk and energy. Linking WebView2, WKWebView or WebKitGTK at run time keeps a minimal app under 600 KB, at the price of platform differences.

choices.choice: A Rust core that owns all system access
choices.why: Rust’s ownership model gives memory and thread safety, and making the core the only process with full operating-system access lets it inspect and filter every message from the web view.
Tauri 2 needed finer control for plugins and mobile, so capability files grant named permissions to specific windows or web views, following the principle of least privilege.
Putting the code under the Commons Conservancy means it can’t be taken away or turned into paid open-core features.
